opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest takeaway is that it's encouraging but you have to read it with the right context. We trained this model with a fairly modest budget. It's about three and a half billion parameters, trained on something like 800 billion tokens, and it was really a single shot. We didn't have the compute to run lots of ablations or tune the data mixture the way a big lab would. So comparing it to the OLMo models is useful, because OLMo is one of the few fully open efforts where you know the data and the training setup. That makes it a fairer baseline than comparing against closed models trained on many trillions of tokens.

What we see is that when you let the model iterate more in its latent space, so you scale up the recurrence at test time, performance on reasoning-heavy benchmarks keeps improving. On things like math and some of the reasoning tasks it gets competitive with, and in places better than, OLMo models that saw a lot more data or have more parameters. On more knowledge-heavy benchmarks, where you just need to have memorized facts, the extra thinking doesn't help nearly as much, and that's actually what you'd expect. You can't reason your way to a fact you never stored.

So to me the main takeaway isn't "we beat OLMo." It's that depth recurrence gives you a different axis for spending compute. Instead of only scaling parameters or writing out long chains of thought in tokens, you can let the model think longer internally, and that seems to buy real gains on tasks that need computation. Whether it holds up at much larger scale with a properly tuned recipe is the open question, and that's what I'd most like to see tested.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the comparison to OLMo was really the one we cared about most, because OLMo is the closest thing to an apples-to-apples baseline. They're fully open, they train on open data, and OLMo-1B and the 7B models are trained on token budgets that overlap with ours. So when we line up Huginn, our 3.5 billion parameter recurrent model, against those, we're not comparing against some mystery model trained on who-knows-what.

And the headline for me is that we trained on about 800 billion tokens, which by modern standards is really not a lot, and the model lands in a range where on things like ARC, HellaSwag, the general reasoning-type benchmarks, it's competitive with OLMo-7B, which saw a couple of trillion tokens. On the more knowledge-heavy stuff like TriviaQA or SciQ, we're weaker, and honestly that's exactly what you'd expect. Recurrence gives you more compute per token at test time, it doesn't give you more facts. Facts live in parameters, and we have fewer parameters and fewer tokens of exposure. So that split in the results was actually kind of reassuring, because it matches the story we were telling ourselves about what the architecture should and shouldn't help with.

Where it really separates is on the reasoning and math side. On GSM8K, for example, with the recurrent depth we get a number that's just far beyond what a fixed-depth model of that size trained on that data would get, and far beyond the OLMo models of comparable training budget. And the key thing is we're not doing anything special there. It's the same pretraining data, no chain-of-thought fine-tuning, no verifiers. The model just gets to iterate its latent state more times before committing to a token.

I'd also say we're careful not to over-read this. It's a single model, a single training run, and we had our own share of instability early on, so I don't want to claim this is a clean scaling law result. What I take away is more modest: that you can spend training compute in a different dimension than parameters and tokens, in depth that's unrolled at test time, and get a model that holds its own against a well-engineered baseline in the same league, while behaving qualitatively differently. The OLMo numbers are the sanity check that says this isn't a toy.

astra-6.text:
The encouraging takeaway is that recurrence seems to be a competitive way to use compute. Relative to the OLMo series, the benchmark results suggest that you can get useful performance by repeatedly applying the same parameters, rather than always adding more distinct layers.

But I’d be careful about turning that into a claim that recurrence is universally better. These comparisons depend on the training data, the training budget, and how much compute you spend at inference. For me, the interesting question is whether additional recurrent steps translate into better answers. That gives us another way to scale a model’s computation without increasing its parameter count.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the encouraging takeaway is that recurrence can be a competitive way to use compute. Relative to the OLMo series, we see that you can get strong benchmark performance by reusing the same parameters across multiple computational steps, rather than making every layer a separate set of parameters.

But I’d be careful about turning that into a blanket claim that the recurrent model is better. The comparison depends on whether you’re matching parameter count, training compute, or inference compute. Reusing parameters makes the model compact, but those recurrent steps still cost computation. So, for me, the interesting result is that this is a viable architectural direction—and that it gives us another way to trade computation for capability.
